{"id": "5b7eb65e-e255-4ad3-8a00-360be087f825", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_pwKPdvnN1kucmyKZkdHW0A", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"Find the changes that could explain the symptoms, or confirm whether and when a specific change happened.\\\\n\\\\n## CloudTrail: `lookup_cloudtrail_events`\\\\n\\\\nCloudTrail calls through `use_aws` are blocked; `lookup_cloudtrail_events` is the route. It returns management events from the last 90 days, newest first, for one account and region per call.\\\\n\\\\n- Each call returns at most about 10,000 characters of events. Every event carries its full CloudTrailEvent JSON, so a call often holds only a handful of events. When it stops early it returns `continuation_timestamp`; pass that as the next `end_time` to page to older events.\\\\n- With no attribute, the tool returns only write events (`ReadOnly` is `false`), which is what a change timeline needs. LookupEvents takes one attribute per call, so passing `attribute_key` and `attribute_value` (EventSource, ResourceName, Username, EventName and so on) replaces that default, and read-only calls then share the size cap with the writes. Use an attribute to follow one resource, user or event name.\\\\n- Narrow before you page: exclude noisy event names and use windows of about 15 minutes. Excluded events do not count toward the size cap. `jmespath_filter` runs after the cap, so it shrinks the output but does not return more events.\\\\n- Passing `exclude_event_names` replaces the default exclusions (`CreateLogStream`, `Invoke`, `InvokeExecution`, `UpdateInstanceInformation`, `PutObject`); include them again if you still want them dropped.\\\\n- LookupEvents allows 2 requests per second per account and region, and one tool call may page several times, so run at most 2 CloudTrail calls at once.\\\\n- Start near the symptom onset and work backward until you find changes that address the question or have covered the requested timeframe.\\\\n\\\\nKubernetes events come from `use_kubectl`. RDS `describe_events` covers only the last 14 days; for an older window, use CloudTrail.\\\\n\\\\n## Judging a change\\\\n\\\\nA change during the incident window matters only if it relates to the investigative question or explains a symptom. {"id": "2cc01c20-6673-474e-81fa-40b1cd82fbab", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Account 012345678901_1 has two IAM users. `llmops-demo-admin` is AT RISK because it has used Bedrock. `llmops-lf-apikey-user` is CAPABLE-BUT-UNUSED, though that rests on weaker evidence. I couldn't pull IAM service-last-accessed data, which the customer asked for, because the tool blocks `generate_service_last_accessed_details`. I used access-key last-used data and CloudTrail instead.

## Organization and SCPs
- The account is in organization `o-0ziep4jkkh`, with all features enabled and SCPs enabled. The management account is 111122223333.
- I couldn't list the SCPs attached to this account. `organizations:ListPoliciesForTarget` was denied for the agent's role. Run that call, or `ListPolicies`, from the management account.

## IAM users (2 total)

| Item | `llmops-demo-admin` | `llmops-lf-apikey-user` |
|---|---|---|

| Console access | No (no login profile) | No (no login profile) |

| Service-specific credential | None | One for `bedrock.amazonaws.com` (a Bedrock API key), Active, created 2026-11-05, expires 2026-12-05 |

| Directly attached managed policies | None | None |
| Inline policies | None | `read-only-catalog`, which allows only `bedrock:ListFoundationModels` on `*` |
| Permission boundary | None shown | None shown |
| Can use Bedrock? | Yes. `AdministratorAccess` (`*:*`) implicitly includes all Bedrock actions. | Yes, but only `bedrock:ListFoundationModels`. |
| Has used Bedrock? | Yes. CloudTrail shows at least 5 `bedrock:Converse` calls on 2026-11-24 between 12:25:16 and 12:26:47 UTC. | No evidence found |
| Classification | **AT RISK** | **CAPABLE-BUT-UNUSED** |

- **`llmops-demo-admin`:** the SCP would break this user's active Bedrock workload.
- **`llmops-lf-apikey-user`:** its Bedrock API key is still active, so the SCP would block it if it were used. The IAM policy gives it a very narrow permission, so even a key-based call can only list foundation models. The user's tags are `llmops-eval=standing` and `llmops-eval-fault=bc-cred-apikey`, which suggest it is a test or evaluation fixture.

## Caveats
- **No service-last-accessed data.** `generate_service_last_accessed_details` and the matching get call were denied by policy, so I have no last-authentication date or action-level data for Bedrock. The access key's last-used record and CloudTrail stand in for it.
- **CloudTrail coverage is limited.** I only checked us-east-1, over the last 24 hours for `llmops-demo-admin` and since 2026-11-05 for `llmops-lf-apikey-user`. I used `lookup_cloudtrail_events`, which covers management events only. It found nothing for `llmops-lf-apikey-user`. Calls made with a Bedrock API key may be logged under a different identity string, and data-event or other-region calls would not show. Treat "unused" for this user as likely but unconfirmed.

I got groups and policies from `get_account_authorization_details` instead, which returned the full policy documents. Permission boundaries come from `get_user`, which shows none.
- **Tracking window.** IAM last-accessed data covers about 400 days for management actions. Bedrock is a newer service, and last-accessed data may not cover every Bedrock action, such as inference calls.
- **Roles are out of scope.** The SCP as described applies to users only. Roles are not checked here, so Bedrock workloads running on roles would be unaffected.
- **Prefix coverage.** Only `bedrock:*` was observed in use. Confirm the SCP also covers `bedrock-agent`, `bedrock-agentcore` and `bedrock-runtime`, with the right IAM prefixes. Bedrock's runtime actions use the `bedrock:` prefix, such as `bedrock:InvokeModel` and `bedrock:Converse`.
- **Account-wide IAM check.** No IAM user, group or policy in the account was missed, since `get_account_authorization_details` returned `IsTruncated: false`.

## Suggested next steps
- Run `generate_service_last_accessed_details` with ACTION_LEVEL granularity from an account with IAM access, or have the policy block lifted.
- Check CloudTrail for the `llmops-lf-apikey-user` API key in the other Bedrock regions.
- List the existing SCPs from the management account.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

It returns management events from the last 90 days, newest first, for one account and region per call.\\\\n\\\\n- Each call returns at most about 10,000 characters of events. Every event carries its full CloudTrailEvent JSON, so a call often holds only a handful of events. When it stops early it returns `continuation_timestamp`; pass that as the next `end_time` to page to older events.\\\\n- With no attribute, the tool returns only write events (`ReadOnly` is `false`), which is what a change timeline needs. LookupEvents takes one attribute per call, so passing `attribute_key` and `attribute_value` (EventSource, ResourceName, Username, EventName and so on) replaces that default, and read-only calls then share the size cap with the writes. Use an attribute to follow one resource, user or event name.\\\\n- Narrow before you page: exclude noisy event names and use windows of about 15 minutes. Excluded events do not count toward the size cap. `jmespath_filter` runs after the cap, so it shrinks the output but does not return more events.\\\\n- Passing `exclude_event_names` replaces the default exclusions (`CreateLogStream`, `Invoke`, `InvokeExecution`, `UpdateInstanceInformation`, `PutObject`); include them again if you still want them dropped.\\\\n- LookupEvents allows 2 requests per second per account and region, and one tool call may page several times, so run at most 2 CloudTrail calls at once.\\\\n- Start near the symptom onset and work backward until you find changes that address the question or have covered the requested timeframe.\\\\n\\\\nKubernetes events come from `use_kubectl`. RDS `describe_events` covers only the last 14 days; for an older window, use CloudTrail.\\\\n\\\\n## Judging a change\\\\n\\\\nA change during the incident window matters only if it relates to the investigative question or explains a symptom. It runs one Logs Insights query against one log group and polls for about 30 seconds; a query still running after that returns an error, so narrow the time range or the filter and retry.\\\\n\\\\nA tool result larger than about 10K tokens (roughly 35K characters) is replaced by a short preview. Keep `limit` small (5 to 20) when you return raw records, and use `stats` or `pattern` to look at volume.\\\\n\\\\nLogs Insights details that are easy to get wrong:\\\\n- `sort` cannot take a function call such as `count()` or `bin(1m)`; alias it in `stats` and sort on the alias: `stats count() as n by bin(1m) as t | sort t`.\\\\n- Compare `@timestamp` with a number only inside `filter`; in `fields`, `stats` or `by` the comparison is a type mismatch.\\\\n- Convert times with the `datetime` tool rather than by hand; hand-computed Unix seconds can be a whole year off.\\\\n- A query whose window ends before a log group was created fails with \\\\\"end date is before the log group\\'s creation time\\\\\". `describe_log_groups` shows each group\\'s `creationTime`, so list an unfamiliar set of groups before querying it.\\\\n- `pattern @message | anomaly` groups messages into patterns and keeps only the statistically unusual ones, which makes it a cheap first look at a busy log group. `pattern` cannot be combined with `stats`.\\\\n- In a regex, `|` means OR, so `(error|500)` matches every \\\\\"500\\\\\" in timestamps and IDs. Match status codes in context, for example `status[:\\\\\\\\s]*\\\\\\\\b5\\\\\\\\d{2}\\\\\\\\b`.\\\\n- A `stats count() by bin(1m)` query over a range that spans the baseline and the incident compares a pattern\\'s frequency in one call.\\\\n\\\\nMore query patterns: [./references/query-examples.md](./references/query-examples.md).\\\\n\\\\n## Baseline and stopping\\\\n\\\\nA pattern that is about as frequent in a healthy window as in the incident window is pre-existing noise, not an incident signal. {"id": "542dbd5a-bb77-4768-b79e-1c6d6519df62", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Account 012345678901_1 has one IAM user that really calls Bedrock: `llmops-demo-admin`. It is still calling Bedrock today, so a blanket deny for IAM users would break it. A second IAM user, `llmops-lf-apikey-user`, holds a Bedrock API key but has made no calls I could find.

## Data sources and coverage

- **Bedrock model invocation logging** is on, in us-east-1 only (CloudWatch log group `/llmops-demo/bedrock-invocations`).
  - It holds 29,017 records, from 2026-10-15 21:48 to 2026-11-25 08:16 UTC. It is the main source for who called what.
  - It records the caller ARN, operation, model and region. It does not record source IP or user agent.
- **CloudTrail** `LookupEvents` covers the last 90 days of management events.
  - Converse and InvokeModel calls show up in it as `bedrock.amazonaws.com` management events, with IP and user agent.
  - I searched us-east-1 in detail. For us-west-2 and eu-west-1 I only spot-checked.
  - I did not search other regions.

## Principals that called Bedrock (invocation log, us-east-1, 2026-10-15 to 2026-11-25)

| Principal | Type | Actions and models | Calls | First seen | Last seen | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `user/llmops-demo-admin` | **IAMUser** | Converse (sonnet-5 4,191, nova-lite 73, haiku-4.5, llama3-8b, nova-2-lite), InvokeModel (haiku-4.5, nova-lite) | about 4,270 | 10-15 | **11-24 12:26** | See below |
| `assumed-role/Admin/<alias>-sandbox` and `sandbox-internal-name` | AssumedRole (federated) | Converse and ConverseStream: sonnet-5, gpt-5.6-terra, nova-lite, opus-4-8 | about 18,100 across 7 sessions | 10-16 | 11-25 08:16 | Not captured in the log; the CloudTrail check did not cover these |
| `assumed-role/llmops-eval-runner/AWSCodeBuild-*` | AssumedRole (CodeBuild) | Converse, gpt-5.6-terra | about 5,000 across 49 sessions | 10-26 | 11-17 | CodeBuild |
| `llmops-lf-*-app-role`, `llmops-lf-gr-*`, `llmops-lf-gh-*` and similar (about 30 roles) | AssumedRole (Lambda) | Converse, ConverseStream and InvokeModel: nova-lite, nova-2-lite, haiku-4.5, llama3-8b | 8 to 96 each | 11-05 | 11-25 06:03 | Lambda (daily run around 06:00 UTC) |
| `llmops-lf-kbrole`, `llmops-demo-kb-role` | AssumedRole (Bedrock Knowledge Base) | InvokeModel with titan-embed-text-v2 | 188 and 25 | 10-15 | 11-25 | Bedrock service |
| `llmops-demo-sagemaker-exec` | AssumedRole (SageMaker) | Converse, sonnet-5 | 175 | 10-18 | 10-18 | SageMaker |
| `AgentCoreRole-cost_estimator_agent` | AssumedRole (AgentCore) | Converse | 2 | 10-15 | 10-22 | AgentCore |
| `llmops-lf-kbrole-noread`, `llmops-lf-mkt-probe-role`, `llmops-lf-app-oldsdk-role` | AssumedRole | Converse and InvokeModel, minor | 2 to 11 each | 11-05 | 11-16 | Not checked |

- **Root:** I found no root calls in the invocation log or the CloudTrail samples. Logs Insights surfaced no root ARN.
- **Federated user:** I found no `FederatedUser` principals.
- **Roles that chain from IAM users:** I found none.
  - The Lambda app roles are assumed by `lambda.amazonaws.com`. I confirmed this for `llmops-lf-gr-support-app-role`.
  - `llmops-eval-runner` trusts only `codebuild.amazonaws.com`.
  - `Admin` trusts only sandbox account 727820809195 with an external ID.
  - I did not read the trust policies of every role.

## IAM-user findings that would break

### `[redacted ARN]`

- **Calls:** Converse and InvokeModel, with the models listed in the table above. It also runs `ListFoundationModels` and `GetModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` (CloudTrail, 2026-11-24 12:05, in eu-west-1 and us-west-2).
- **Window:** active from 2026-10-15 to 2026-11-24 12:26 UTC. The access key `AKIA<key id>` was last used 2026-11-24 12:26 on `bedrock` in us-east-1.
- **Source IPs:**
  - 49.207.206.77 (2026-10-15, a "llmops-demo-generator/1.0" Boto3 client).
  - 49.207.216.85 (2026-11-05 and 2026-11-24).
- **User agents:** Boto3 and Botocore with `app/kiro-ide`, on macOS arm64 and Python 3.12 to 3.14. This is a developer workstation using a long-lived access key.
- **Services:**
  - `bedrock.amazonaws.com` called Converse as this user on 2026-10-15 22:00, using the user's credentials. It came from a guardrail-enabled inference-profile call, and the event has `invokedBy` set to `bedrock.amazonaws.com`.
  - The same user also made `PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` calls on 2026-10-15 21:48, which turned logging on.
  - It also created the Bedrock API key for `llmops-lf-apikey-user` on 2026-11-05 (`CreateServiceSpecificCredential`).
  - It also calls `aidevops.amazonaws.com` `CreateChat`, which is DevOps Agent, on 2026-11-24.
- **Region:** CloudTrail shows `Converse` in eu-west-1 on 2026-11-05 08:26. The invocation log is us-east-1 only, so it would not show that call. Some us-east-1 calls were served from us-west-2 through cross-region inference.

### `[redacted ARN]`

- It has no access keys but has one Active Bedrock API key (service-specific credential), created 2026-11-05 and expiring 2026-12-05.
- CloudTrail lookup by this username returned zero events. I saw no use in the invocation log either.
- **Caveat:** Bedrock API key calls may be logged under a different principal or with an unclear identity. This user is still the owner of a live Bedrock key, so a deny would revoke that key's access.

One log record (2026-10-15 21:48:54) has no `identity.arn`. It looks like the `PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration` test message.

## Other regions

- **us-west-2:** CloudTrail shows only read and list events. All of them are from the DevOps Agent role session `monitorAssociationRoleSession`, plus `llmops-demo-admin` on 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-24. I saw no model invocations there.
- **eu-west-1:** There was one Converse by IAM-user session `llmops-lf-app-wrongregion` on 2026-11-25 06:03. There was also one Converse by `llmops-demo-admin` on 2026-11-05.

## Not visible or not done

- **CloudTrail:** `LookupEvents` returns management events only, for 90 days.
  - The trail "sandbox-internal-name" (S3, multi-region) has no custom event selectors, so it has no data events. The "bedrock-runtime" data events (InvokeModel and similar) are not logged.
  - The org trails have custom selectors, but they sit in management account 111122223333. I could not read them.
  - Each call returns about 5 events, so I could not page through the roughly 4,000+ Converse events. Counts come from the invocation log. The IP and user-agent details come from sampled events, newest and oldest only. Other IPs or agents may exist for the IAM user between those dates.
- **Invocation log:**
  - It exists only in us-east-1. Calls in other regions, such as the eu-west-1 `wrongregion` call, are not in it.
  - It starts on 2026-10-15, so there is nothing for the first seven weeks of the 90-day window.
- **DevOps Agent noise:** read calls from `monitorAssociationRoleSession` dominate `bedrock.amazonaws.com` CloudTrail output. It is the DevOps Agent's own service role. An SCP denying Bedrock to IAM users would not block assumed-role sessions, so this is not directly affected.
- **Not examined:**
  - Bedrock-agent (`bedrock-agent.amazonaws.com`) events: none returned apart from those listed.
  - S3 invocation-log delivery: the config uses CloudWatch only, so I did not check S3.
  - Regions beyond us-east-1, us-west-2 and eu-west-1.
  - Whether `Admin` sessions chain from IAM users: they come from sandbox account 727820809195 with an external ID, not from any IAM user in this account.

## Suggested next steps

- Check for Bedrock API key usage outside CloudTrail, and decide what to do with `llmops-lf-apikey-user` before the SCP goes live.
- Decide whether `llmops-demo-admin` should move to a role, or be explicitly exempted in the SCP (for example with a `NotPrincipal`-style condition on `aws:PrincipalArn`), since it is in active use.
- Run the SCP as a test in a sandbox OU first.
- Search CloudTrail in more regions, and in the org-level S3 trail, for `llmops-demo-admin` and `llmops-lf-apikey-user`.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "b5c9562f-abe4-4fa3-a920-987aacb048b5", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_3yWuACR0DBYSEIxQeLgEbP", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"Find the changes that could explain the symptoms, or confirm whether and when a specific change happened.\\\\n\\\\n## CloudTrail: `lookup_cloudtrail_events`\\\\n\\\\nCloudTrail calls through `use_aws` are blocked; `lookup_cloudtrail_events` is the route. It returns management events from the last 90 days, newest first, for one account and region per call.\\\\n\\\\n- Each call returns at most about 10,000 characters of events. Every event carries its full CloudTrailEvent JSON, so a call often holds only a handful of events. When it stops early it returns `continuation_timestamp`; pass that as the next `end_time` to page to older events.\\\\n- With no attribute, the tool returns only write events (`ReadOnly` is `false`), which is what a change timeline needs. LookupEvents takes one attribute per call, so passing `attribute_key` and `attribute_value` (EventSource, ResourceName, Username, EventName and so on) replaces that default, and read-only calls then share the size cap with the writes. Use an attribute to follow one resource, user or event name.\\\\n- Narrow before you page: exclude noisy event names and use windows of about 15 minutes. Excluded events do not count toward the size cap. `jmespath_filter` runs after the cap, so it shrinks the output but does not return more events.\\\\n- Passing `exclude_event_names` replaces the default exclusions (`CreateLogStream`, `Invoke`, `InvokeExecution`, `UpdateInstanceInformation`, `PutObject`); include them again if you still want them dropped.\\\\n- LookupEvents allows 2 requests per second per account and region, and one tool call may page several times, so run at most 2 CloudTrail calls at once.\\\\n- Start near the symptom onset and work backward until you find changes that address the question or have covered the requested timeframe.\\\\n\\\\nKubernetes events come from `use_kubectl`. RDS `describe_events` covers only the last 14 days; for an older window, use CloudTrail.\\\\n\\\\n## Judging a change\\\\n\\\\nA change during the incident window matters only if it relates to the investigative question or explains a symptom. When a change modified a resource that is now degraded, describe the resulting state, not just the event, and say whether that state deterministically stops the resource from working (an emptied security group, revoked IAM permissions, a black-hole route). A deterministic block takes precedence over load-based explanations, and timing alone is no reason to dismiss it.\\\\n\\\\nStop when the question is settled: you have found changes that address it, or
